young.html: Arthur Eddington was an English astronomer who could make the hardest ideas sound like an adventure story. In 1933 he wrote a little book about a big surprise: the galaxies are rushing away from us, and from each other. The whole universe is getting bigger.

How can that be? Picture a balloon with dots drawn on it. Blow it up. Every dot moves away from every other dot, and no dot is the center. A dot twice as far away moves away twice as fast. The galaxies behave the same way.

young.name: gb-balloon
young.cap: Press Inflate. Tap any dot to stand on it: all the others move away, and the farther ones move faster. The same is true from every dot.

young.html: Balloon universe. Draw 8 or 10 dots on a balloon with a marker, with a grown-up’s help. Blow it up a little and measure, with a string, the distance from one dot to its neighbors. Blow it up more and measure again. Which distances grew the most? Now pick a different dot. Does the universe look different from there?

Astronomers learned this by looking at the light of far-off galaxies. Their light is stretched toward the red end of the rainbow, the way the sound of a passing car’s engine drops in pitch as it drives away. The farther the galaxy, the more its light is stretched.

full.html: Sir Arthur Eddington (1882–1944) was Plumian Professor of Astronomy at Cambridge and the leading English-speaking interpreter of Einstein. In 1919 he led the eclipse expedition to the island of Príncipe, off West Africa, whose photographs of stars near the darkened Sun helped confirm general relativity. He worked out much of how stars shine (The Internal Constitution of the Stars, 1926) and wrote popular books that sold widely.

The Expanding Universe (Cambridge University Press, 1933) grew from a public lecture he gave at the meeting of the International Astronomical Union in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in September 1932. It is a short, witty account of a discovery only a few years old.
This book was first published in 1933, so it is still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of it. Everything here is our own summary. Look for it in a library (it was reprinted many times).

items: From 1912 on, Vesto Slipher measured the spectra of faint spiral nebulae and found that most of them were moving away from us, fast.
In the 1920s Edwin Hubble showed these nebulae are galaxies far outside our own Milky Way.
In 1929 Hubble found that the farther a galaxy is, the faster it recedes: speed is proportional to distance. This is Hubble’s law, $v = H_0 d$.

Meanwhile the theorists had found that Einstein’s equations allow a universe that expands. Alexander Friedmann (1922) and Georges Lemaître (1927) had worked it out. Eddington helped bring Lemaître’s paper to English readers in 1931.

full.name: gb-balloon
full.cap: A two-dimensional model: the galaxies sit on the surface of the balloon. Speed divided by distance is the same for every pair, which is Hubble’s law.

full.html: Eddington explains the expansion as a property of space itself, not galaxies flying through a fixed space. In Einstein’s theory the universe can be finite but without an edge, like the surface of a sphere, and that surface can grow. He describes the cosmical constant, a term Einstein had added to his equations, as a kind of cosmic repulsion that pushes the galaxies apart, and he hopes to calculate it from the theory of the atom. He did not like the idea of a sudden beginning; he favored a universe that had rested in balance for ages before it began, slowly, to expand.
The book also faces a puzzle. Using Hubble’s measurements, the expansion seemed to have started only about 2 billion years earlier, less than the age geologists were finding for the Earth.

full.title: Hubble’s law
full.q: A galaxy is 100 megaparsecs away (one megaparsec is about 3.26 million light-years). Today’s value of the Hubble constant is about 70 km/s per megaparsec. How fast is it receding?

full.title: How old is the universe?
full.q: If the galaxies have always receded at their present speeds, they were all together a time $1/H_0$ ago. With $H_0$ in km/s per megaparsec, that time in billions of years is about $978 \div H_0$. Compare Hubble’s 1929 value, about 500, with today’s, about 70.
steps: The careful modern figure, allowing for changes in the rate, is 13.8 billion years.
full.a: About 2 billion years then; about 14 billion now.

full.html: In an expanding universe, every observer sees the same thing: everything else moving away, with speed proportional to distance. There is no center of the expansion, just as no dot is the center of a balloon’s surface.

Picturing the galaxies as fragments flying out from one spot in space, like a bomb. The expansion is of space itself, everywhere at once. That is also why far galaxies can recede faster than light without breaking relativity’s speed limit, which applies to motion through space.

The age puzzle was solved in the 1950s, when Walter Baade and others found that the distances to galaxies had been badly underestimated. The Hubble constant dropped, and the age of the universe grew past the age of the Earth. Eddington’s preferred slow start lost out: the evidence of the 1960s, above all the faint microwave glow left over from a hot, dense early universe (discovered in 1965), supported a big bang beginning of the kind Lemaître had proposed. Eddington’s attempt to calculate the cosmical constant from atomic numbers was not accepted by other physicists. But the book’s picture of a universe of galaxies in an expanding space is the one astronomers still use, and in 1998 they found that the expansion is speeding up, which brought back something like Einstein’s and Eddington’s cosmical constant.

items: Ptolemy and Copernicus, earlier on this ladder, argued about what is at the center. Eddington’s universe has no center at all.
Einstein’s Relativity, the rung before, ends with thoughts on whether the universe is finite. Eddington shows what the equations made of that question.
Planck and Bohr, the next rungs, built the quantum physics that Eddington tried, without success, to join to cosmology.
If everything is moving away from us, why aren’t we at the center?
Eddington disliked the idea of a beginning. Should a scientist’s taste in ideas count for anything?
What would it mean for the universe to be finite but have no edge?

questions: What is something you once thought was standing still but turned out to be moving?
On a balloon, every dot sees the others moving away. Why does that mean there’s no center?
Astronomers learned the universe is expanding from the color of starlight. What else can light tell us?
Eddington’s numbers made the universe younger than the Earth. What would you do if your measurements gave an impossible answer?
Why do you think Eddington spent so much time writing for ordinary readers?
